transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon.
President Trump has responded to the resignation of NVIDIA CEO Jason Jensen Wong, saying he
wants former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take over Wong's job.
Wong has been close to the president, even traveling with him to China as the White House
considered AI policy.
NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben reports.
On social media this morning, Trump wrote that Wong has done "a fantastic job."
He added, "There is only one man to take his place, Tim Cook of Apple.
A legend replaces a legend."
Wong announced his resignation after news reports alleging that he had had an extramarital
affair with one of the company's clients, who U.S. intelligence officials concluded
had been recruited by China's top spy agency.
Wong has had the president's ear for much of this term, demonstrated in September when
Trump called Wong's phone while Wong was on stage at a conference.
He also joined Trump on a state visit to the U.K. last year and to China this year.
Danielle Kurtzleben, NPR News, The White House.
A group of key voters in North Carolina says expectations are low for what Democrats can
achieve next year in a divided government.
NPR's Ashley Lopez observed two online focus groups with these voters this week.
The group of voters say they don't think Democrats will be able to get much done because President
Trump will be a major obstacle.
Rick, who participated in the focus groups under the condition his last name would not
be used, said he's also worried Democrats will spend too much time focusing on investigating
Trump and his family.
"It doesn't really matter because there are people in the middle that are being forgotten
and can't afford gas and health care."
The groups were made up of 14 voters who supported President Biden in 2020 and then Trump in
2024.
Exit polls show most Americans want to see accountability, but these voters say they
want to see Democrats prioritize lowering prices.
Ashley Lopez, NPR News.
A building collapse next to a construction site in Brooklyn, New York, has killed two
children and six adults.
New York mayors Zoran Mondani praised the first responders and the construction workers
who help rescue survivors within moments of the collapse.
Mayor Mondani also says other sites associated with the construction company are being thoroughly
examined.
"There are five main entities involved with this construction site who are associated
with approximately 100 other sites across the city.
Our Department of Buildings is commencing sweeps of those sites today."
In addition to the eight people killed in the building collapse, at least 17 others
were injured, including three firefighters.
U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Whitcoff are heading to Ireland to meet with Ukrainian
President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Kushner and Whitcoff just wrapped up talks in Moscow with Russian President Volodymyr
Putin about ending Russia's war against Ukraine.
The war began in 2022.
You're listening to NPR.
The Education Department has finalized new rules for college accreditors.
As NPR's Corey Turner reports, some higher education experts worry these changes could
give the department the power to oversee political speech on campus.
Colleges pay third-party accreditors to certify the quality of things like curriculum and
faculty.
The Education Department sets the ground rules.
And one big new change to those rules says accreditors must now ensure that students
are exposed to a range of viewpoints on campus.
Multiple higher education experts tell NPR that could open the door for the department
to police campus speech.
The Education Department disputes that, though, and tells NPR the change is about making sure
differing perspectives can be debated openly and fairly.
But in a 2023 speech, then-former President Trump said overhauling accreditation would
be his "secret weapon" to reclaim our once-great educational institutions from the radical
left.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
It was once the fastest ocean liner on the seas, setting a record on its first voyage
back in 1952.
Now it is the world's largest artificial reef.
The SS United States was sunk last night to settle on the seafloor in the Gulf of Mexico
between Panama City and Pensacola, Florida.
The $13.5 million project is designed to attract more divers and fishing enthusiasts while
also creating a home for tuna, marlin, and swordfish.
The project also saves that ship from becoming scrap metal.
I'm Linda Kenyon.
NPR News, in Washington.
